What you will practice · Choose your pace

What you will practice

  • Clarify scope, distinguish acknowledgment from approval, and confirm conditions.
  • Probe evidence, make a concession without surrendering the decision, and set a conduct boundary.
  • Define decision rights, invite recommendations, and delegate within explicit limits.
  • Offer bounded alternatives, use conditional commitments, and distinguish a forecast from a promise.
  • Manage turn-taking, interrupt constructively, paraphrase accurately, and close a hybrid meeting.

Choose your pace

Quick practice · 15 minutes: complete one short exchange, check the explanations, and read both roles aloud.

Extended practice · two or three sittings: check the case facts, study the vocabulary and phrases, complete the longer conversation, then rehearse the follow-up exchange.

Level guide: designed for intermediate to advanced learners. B1 learners can start with the short exchanges and supplied phrases; B2 learners can complete the cloze conversations; C1 learners can focus on the distinctions in the language checks. These are teaching suggestions, not a certified level assessment.

Professional communication notes

Directness, disagreement, and local norms

Do not infer intent from volume or speed alone. Test the claim, watch the response, and distinguish a sharp challenge from personal contempt.

Challenge the claim
"Which assumption is wrong?" keeps the discussion on something that can be checked. Accepting one criticism does not require abandoning the whole proposal.
Set a behavioral boundary
"Keep the criticism on the estimate, not the people." A colleague's stated good intention does not erase an insult or repeated interruption.
Check the local rule
First names, humor, and informal meetings do not tell you who can approve spending. Ask which decisions are yours and which need approval.
Make room for a different pace
Some colleagues think aloud; others want time to read before speaking. Use a pre-read, a clear speaking order, and a later input route rather than equating speed with competence.
Separate rapport from commitment
A friendly "sounds good" can support a direction without accepting a deadline. Confirm the deliverable, owner, condition, and time.
Name what a deadline means
"Friday" may refer to different time zones or different versions of a report. State the clock time, location, and whether the figures are provisional or verified.

Nationality is not a personality test. Role, power, language confidence, professional training, and company norms also shape an exchange. Do not normalize threats, discrimination, or intimidation as a cultural style; use appropriate workplace support and reporting routes.

Your goal

Clarify scope, distinguish acknowledgment from approval, and confirm conditions.

This lesson in the book, page 4 ↗

A Read the situation

When "fine" is not a green light

Aiko recorded agreement to a Monday product launch after hearing that the plan was "fine." Jordan then sent a staffing concern. The branch has six trained people; the launch plan needs eight. Two more people may finish training on Friday, but completion is not yet confirmed. Aiko can authorize the branch launch after the staffing check.

Launch tracker / Wednesday, 11:00 a.m.
ItemCurrent record
Launch dateMonday, proposed
Trained staff6 confirmed; 8 required
Friday training2 places booked; completion pending
Decision ownerAiko, after Jordan reports the staffing check

Aiko: International branch manager / Jordan: US-based operations lead

Check the facts · 3 questions

Choose the answer supported by the briefing. Do not assume that a proposed action has already happened.

1. Which statement can Aiko enter as confirmed now?

Answer and explanation

Correct: C. Six people have completed training.

  1. A. Monday is approved subject to training.The date is proposed. Aiko has not yet authorized even a conditional launch.
  2. B. Jordan has cleared the launch date.Jordan checks staffing; the tracker assigns the decision to Aiko.
  3. C. Six people have completed training.The tracker confirms six completed trainees, not eight.
  4. D. Eight people have places on Friday.Only two places are booked for Friday; six people are already trained.
2. Which next step preserves the decision boundary?

Answer and explanation

Correct: C. Jordan checks staffing; Aiko decides afterward.

  1. A. Both trainees confirm and release the plan.The trainees do not hold launch authority.
  2. B. Jordan checks staffing and authorizes Monday.Checking staffing does not transfer Aiko's decision right.
  3. C. Jordan checks staffing; Aiko decides afterward.Evidence gathering and authorization belong to different people here.
  4. D. Aiko authorizes now and checks Friday.That reverses the stated sequence and treats a prerequisite as a later formality.
3. Jordan says, "The approach is fine." Which follow-up resolves its scope?

Answer and explanation

Correct: B. Does that include Monday, or just the sequence?

  1. A. Can I tell the team you are fully aligned?Fully aligned expands an ambiguous statement instead of clarifying it.
  2. B. Does that include Monday, or just the sequence?The question separates the date from the approach without assigning a motive.
  3. C. Shall I record approval and add your staffing note?That labels the statement approval before establishing whether it was approval.
  4. D. Would a different date make you more comfortable?That assumes the date is the concern before checking what Jordan meant.

B Find the words

Vocabulary and collocations

Acknowledgment confirms that a message was received or understood. Endorsement expresses support. Authorization permits action. Ask which of these the speaker is giving; do not record one as another.

24 field terms and natural word combinations
acknowledgment
A signal that a message has been received or understood.acknowledge receipt
endorsement
An expression of support for a proposal or position.endorse a proposal
authorization
Permission from someone entitled to approve an action.obtain authorization
reservation
A concern that limits or qualifies support.express a reservation
provisional
Not final; subject to a stated check or decision.provisional launch date
dependency
Something that must happen for another action to proceed.resolve a dependency
read-back
A spoken restatement used to check the shared record.give a read-back
sign-off
A formal or agreed approval step.get final sign-off
scope
The limits of what a statement or agreement covers.clarify the scope
conditional agreement
Support that applies only if a requirement is met.record conditional agreement
go/no-go decision
A decision to proceed or stop at a defined checkpoint.make a go/no-go decision
green light
Informal permission to proceed, not merely positive feedback.give the green light
clarification
Additional detail that resolves an unclear meaning.seek clarification
alignment
A shared understanding or compatible direction; not necessarily formal approval.check alignment on the date
pending
Waiting for an event, result, or decision.approval pending review
prerequisite
A requirement that must be met before another action.satisfy a prerequisite
assumption
Something treated as true before it has been established.test an assumption
explicit
Stated directly rather than left for the listener to infer.obtain explicit approval
implicit
Suggested or understood without being stated directly.avoid relying on implicit consent
qualification
A condition or limitation attached to a statement.add a qualification
tentative
Not firmly settled and still open to change.set a tentative date
supersede
Replace an earlier record, instruction, or decision.supersede the earlier minutes
discrepancy
A difference between accounts or records that should match.resolve a discrepancy
in principle
At the level of the general idea, with details still unresolved.agree in principle

"We agree in principle" supports the general idea. "We have authorized the launch" permits an action. A tentative date and a pending decision identify what remains unsettled.

Say it in context · 4 expressions

Capitals show the stressed syllable, not a full pronunciation spelling.

authorization au-thor-i-ZA-tion
We have support for the plan, but no authorization to launch.

Support is not permission.

provisional pro-VI-sion-al
Treat Monday as provisional until Friday's check.

Provisional is not confirmed.

supersede su-per-SEDE
This note supersedes the earlier minutes.

Supersede replaces a record; supplement adds to it.

endorsement en-DORSE-ment
Jordan endorsed the approach, not the date.

Name exactly what is endorsed.

C Notice the language

Acknowledgment is not authorization

A nod, "fine," or "I see" can acknowledge a message without approving the proposed action. This ambiguity is not unique to any nationality. A manager who hears agreement can check it without embarrassing the speaker: identify the precise decision, name any condition, and read back the record. Do not ask whether the colleague is "really committed" when the unresolved issue is staffing.

16 useful phrases, grouped by purpose
Specify the reference
When you say "fine," are you referring to the date or the overall approach?
Separate two meanings
I heard support for the approach, not approval of the date.
State the condition
My support is conditional on having eight trained people.
Check a commitment
Can I record that as a commitment, or is it still a possibility?
Preserve uncertainty
That remains provisional until we complete the staffing check.
Make an indirect question
Could you confirm whether the additional training is complete?
Read back the agreement
Let me read that back so we have the same decision record.
Close the loop
I will send the revised record and ask you to confirm it.
Expose an assumption
I may be reading more into that than you intended.
Limit general agreement
We agree in principle; the staffing condition is still open.
Check the reference
By "ready," do you mean trained, scheduled, or available for the first shift?
Separate response and decision
Please acknowledge receipt separately from confirming approval.
Identify the missing evidence
What evidence would let us change the status from pending to confirmed?
Qualify a date
Monday is our working date, subject to the Friday staffing check.
Replace an inaccurate record
This note supersedes the earlier statement that the date was final.
Check the whole condition
Is there any condition missing from that summary?
6 language and precision notes
Embedded questions
Use "Could you confirm whether the training is complete?" The clause after "whether" has statement order, not "whether is the training complete."
Meaning of "not yet"
"Not yet approved" leaves approval open. "Not approved" can sound like a refusal unless the context makes the pending status clear.
Precision before politeness
"Are we aligned?" is broad. "Are you approving Monday, provided that eight people are trained?" checks an action and its condition.
Name the reference
Replace a vague "that" with the relevant noun: "Do you support the sequence, the date, or both?"
Keep the qualification attached
"We support Monday, provided that eight people are trained" keeps the condition in the same sentence as the support.
Replace rather than add
"This note supersedes the earlier minutes" identifies which record now applies. "Here is another note" leaves that uncertain.
Same purpose, different register

To a colleague: So the approach works; Monday is still open?

In a decision record: The approach is supported. Launch authorization remains pending.

Clarifying politely: I may have read too much into "fine."

Confirming formally: Please confirm whether your agreement includes the proposed date.

D Check your understanding

Choose the precise message

Choose one best answer using the case facts and the stated purpose.

1. Choose a correction to minutes that wrongly say "Monday approved."

Answer and explanation

Correct: A. Monday remains proposed; Aiko will decide after Friday's staffing check.

  1. A. Monday remains proposed; Aiko will decide after Friday's staffing check.This corrects status, decision owner, and prerequisite together.
  2. B. Monday remains supported; the staffing check will follow the launch.It reverses the sequence and leaves approval ambiguous.
  3. C. Monday remains likely; the team will proceed unless someone objects.Likelihood and silence do not provide the required authorization.
  4. D. Monday remains approved; Jordan will add Friday's staffing figures.It preserves the inaccurate approval status.
2. Which sentence distinguishes receipt from approval?

Answer and explanation

Correct: B. I have read the plan; I have not authorized the date.

  1. A. I have seen the plan; go ahead with the proposed date.Go ahead grants the permission the sentence needs to withhold.
  2. B. I have read the plan; I have not authorized the date.Reading acknowledges receipt without implying permission.
  3. C. I have accepted the plan; the date is now in place.Accepted and in place suggest approval, not receipt alone.
  4. D. I have read the plan; please regard the date as settled.This explicitly makes the date final.
3. Two training places are booked. What can the update say?

Answer and explanation

Correct: C. Both places are booked; completion still needs confirmation.

  1. A. Both people are available; training will confirm the date.Availability is not supplied, and training alone does not authorize the date.
  2. B. Both people are confirmed; their assessment will follow later.Confirmed leaves readiness implied before assessment.
  3. C. Both places are booked; completion still needs confirmation.A booking is evidence of a plan, not completion.
  4. D. Both people are ready; their training is scheduled Friday.Ready overstates what a scheduled session establishes.
4. Aiko wants a final check without making Jordan defend his intentions. Choose her line.

Answer and explanation

Correct: A. What condition is missing from that summary?

  1. A. What condition is missing from that summary?It invites a factual correction without judging sincerity.
  2. B. Are you committed enough to make Monday happen?It shifts a staffing condition into a judgment of commitment.
  3. C. Why did you agree if you had a reservation?It assumes Jordan agreed to the date, the disputed point.
  4. D. Can we leave your concern out until Friday?It would hide a condition that affects the record now.

When "fine" is not a green light

Aiko: International branch manager / Jordan: US-based operations lead

Complete the numbered gaps. Use each bank entry once, without changing its form.

  1. Aiko
    Before I send these minutes, can we check one line? I wrote "Monday launch approved." You said the plan was fine yesterday.
  2. Jordan
    The sequence was fine. I still had a 1 about staffing. I thought I mentioned that before we moved on.
  3. Aiko
    You did mention training. I took that as an update, not a condition. That was my mistake.
  4. Jordan
    We have six people trained. We need eight. Two more are booked for Friday, but booking them isn't the same as having them ready.
  5. Aiko
    Right. So Monday stays 2. I'll remove "approved" from the minutes.
  6. Jordan
    Thanks. I don't want the team to cancel anything yet, either. Monday could still work.
  7. Aiko
    Then I'll say we agree 3 on the approach. The date remains open until Friday.
  8. Jordan
    That captures it. Who is going to tell the customer team? They've already asked me whether to send the launch notice.
  9. Aiko
    I will. Preparing the notice is fine; sending it needs my 4. We haven't reached that point.
  10. Jordan
    Good. I can give you the training results Friday afternoon. Do you need anything beyond the completion list?
  11. Aiko
    Yes, please check that all eight are available for the first shift. Training is a 5, not the entire readiness check.
  12. Jordan
    Understood. I'll confirm completion and first-shift availability. If one person doesn't finish, I'll flag that rather than count the booking.
  13. Aiko
    Please do. I'd rather have a clear 6 than leave everyone interpreting "probably."
  14. Jordan
    Agreed. Could you copy me on the corrected minutes? People may still be looking at the first version.
  15. Aiko
    Yes. The new note will 7 the earlier one. I'll put that in the first sentence.
  16. Jordan
    And I'll reply to confirm the staffing wording. That isn't me signing off on the launch, though.
  17. Aiko
    Exactly. I'll keep your 8 of receipt separate from my launch decision.
  18. Jordan
    Then we're clear. Six trained today; two more pending; Monday not yet approved.
  19. Aiko
    That's the 9 I needed. Anything else I have interpreted too strongly?
  20. Jordan
    No. Once you've reviewed the Friday check, you can 10 or move the date. I'll wait for that message.

Answers and explanations
  1. reservation Turn 2. A reservation limits Jordan's support; it does not withdraw support for the sequence.
  2. provisional Turn 5. Provisional keeps the date open until the staffing check and decision.
  3. in principle Turn 7. In principle expresses support for the approach without granting final approval.
  4. authorization Turn 9. Authorization is permission from Aiko, who owns the launch decision.
  5. prerequisite Turn 11. A prerequisite must be met before launch; it is not proof that all other conditions are met.
  6. go/no-go decision Turn 13. A go/no-go decision explicitly determines whether the launch proceeds.
  7. supersede Turn 15. Supersede means replace the inaccurate earlier record, not add another equally valid version.
  8. acknowledgment Turn 17. Acknowledgment of receipt confirms that Jordan received the note; it is not his launch approval.
  9. read-back Turn 19. A read-back restates the shared record so the other person can correct it.
  10. give the green light Turn 20. Give the green light means authorize the launch; this verb phrase fits after can.
Read the complete conversation
  1. Aiko: Before I send these minutes, can we check one line? I wrote "Monday launch approved." You said the plan was fine yesterday.
  2. Jordan: The sequence was fine. I still had a reservation about staffing. I thought I mentioned that before we moved on.
  3. Aiko: You did mention training. I took that as an update, not a condition. That was my mistake.
  4. Jordan: We have six people trained. We need eight. Two more are booked for Friday, but booking them isn't the same as having them ready.
  5. Aiko: Right. So Monday stays provisional. I'll remove "approved" from the minutes.
  6. Jordan: Thanks. I don't want the team to cancel anything yet, either. Monday could still work.
  7. Aiko: Then I'll say we agree in principle on the approach. The date remains open until Friday.
  8. Jordan: That captures it. Who is going to tell the customer team? They've already asked me whether to send the launch notice.
  9. Aiko: I will. Preparing the notice is fine; sending it needs my authorization. We haven't reached that point.
  10. Jordan: Good. I can give you the training results Friday afternoon. Do you need anything beyond the completion list?
  11. Aiko: Yes, please check that all eight are available for the first shift. Training is a prerequisite, not the entire readiness check.
  12. Jordan: Understood. I'll confirm completion and first-shift availability. If one person doesn't finish, I'll flag that rather than count the booking.
  13. Aiko: Please do. I'd rather have a clear go/no-go decision than leave everyone interpreting "probably."
  14. Jordan: Agreed. Could you copy me on the corrected minutes? People may still be looking at the first version.
  15. Aiko: Yes. The new note will supersede the earlier one. I'll put that in the first sentence.
  16. Jordan: And I'll reply to confirm the staffing wording. That isn't me signing off on the launch, though.
  17. Aiko: Exactly. I'll keep your acknowledgment of receipt separate from my launch decision.
  18. Jordan: Then we're clear. Six trained today; two more pending; Monday not yet approved.
  19. Aiko: That's the read-back I needed. Anything else I have interpreted too strongly?
  20. Jordan: No. Once you've reviewed the Friday check, you can give the green light or move the date. I'll wait for that message.

Three more conversations at work

Each short conversation has its own fictional situation and facts.

Reopening the launch agreement

The branch manager follows up on the lesson's launch meeting after receiving a staffing concern.

  1. Branch manager: I recorded agreement when you said the plan was fine. Your email suggests a staffing concern.
  2. Operations lead: I meant the launch sequence looked reasonable, not that we had enough people.
  3. Branch manager: Thank you for the clarification. Which part of my recorded expectation needs correcting?
  4. Operations lead: Please separate support for the sequence from confirmation that staffing is sufficient.
  5. Branch manager: Was your staffing concern already resolved when we finished the meeting?
  6. Operations lead: No. My email raises it because we still need to discuss coverage.
  7. Branch manager: Then my assumption was too broad. I should not have recorded full agreement.
  8. Operations lead: Could we reopen that point before presenting the plan as settled?
  9. Branch manager: Yes. I'll correct the record and invite both colleagues to clarify their positions.
  10. Operations lead: That works. We can discuss coverage without implying that either colleague approved it.
Available does not mean assigned

A separate fictional branch case: a training coordinator has two free hours Thursday, but no assignment has been agreed.

  1. Branch manager: You said you were available Thursday. May I announce you as the workshop facilitator?
  2. Training coordinator: Could you clarify the assignment first? I have two hours free, not an unlimited opening.
  3. Branch manager: I was assuming availability meant a commitment to lead the whole session.
  4. Training coordinator: That wasn't my intention. I need the session length and preparation expectation.
  5. Branch manager: We haven't settled either detail. What can I accurately tell the planning group?
  6. Training coordinator: Say that I have a possible two-hour slot, subject to reviewing the work.
  7. Branch manager: So you haven't accepted facilitation or preparation duties at this stage?
  8. Training coordinator: Correct. Please ask the group to define those duties before requesting confirmation.
  9. Branch manager: I'll bring back a specific request instead of adding your name to the agenda.
  10. Training coordinator: Thanks. Once the scope is clear, I can give you a definite answer.
Whose end of day?

A separate fictional handoff connects offices using Eastern and Pacific time. A request says only 'end of day.'

  1. Branch coordinator: Your request says end of day. Which time zone should we use for this handoff?
  2. Headquarters analyst: I meant Eastern time, but I didn't include a specific hour.
  3. Branch coordinator: Our team uses Pacific time. That leaves room for a different assumption.
  4. Headquarters analyst: You're right. I also need to clarify whether I want preliminary or reviewed numbers.
  5. Branch coordinator: Which version does your next meeting actually require us to supply?
  6. Headquarters analyst: I need reviewed numbers, but I haven't checked when your review finishes.
  7. Branch coordinator: Then let's establish availability before turning that expectation into a deadline.
  8. Headquarters analyst: Could you check the review schedule while I confirm the meeting's cutoff?
  9. Branch coordinator: Yes. We'll agree an exact time and zone after those two checks.
  10. Headquarters analyst: I'll leave the delivery time unconfirmed until we have that clarification.

F Say it

Two scenarios to practice

When "fine" is not a green light
  1. Read turns 1-10 with a partner; insert your selected answers without adding facts.
  2. Switch roles for turns 11-20. Pause after each clarification question until the partner finishes the printed reply.

On your own: read both roles. With a partner: swap roles after the first reading. Use the completed conversation to check any line you need to repeat.

A supplier says "looks good"

Twelve test units are proposed for Tuesday. The supplier has acknowledged the design, but has not confirmed capacity. Maya owns the purchase decision. Ellis will check supplier capacity by Monday noon.

Choose one answer for each gap, then read the exchange in order. Check the explanation after each choice.

Maya: The supplier wrote "looks good." Does that cover the design or the delivery date?

1. Ellis: "The design. Tuesday remains ___."

Answer and explanation

Correct: D. proposed

Proposed is the stated status of Tuesday; the supplier has not committed to it.

2. Maya: "Then please check ___ by Monday noon."

Answer and explanation

Correct: D. capacity

Capacity is the supplier's ability to supply the twelve units, the unresolved factual condition.

Ellis: I will. Shall I place the order if they can supply twelve?

3. Maya: "No. Bring the confirmation to me for ___."

Answer and explanation

Correct: D. approval

Maya retains the purchase decision even after capacity is confirmed.

4. Ellis: "Understood. I'll send an update by noon, even if the supplier's answer is still ___."

Answer and explanation

Correct: B. pending

Pending means the supplier has not yet resolved the question.

Read the complete follow-up exchange
  1. Maya: The supplier wrote "looks good." Does that cover the design or the delivery date?
  2. Ellis: The design. Tuesday remains proposed.
  3. Maya: Then please check capacity by Monday noon.
  4. Ellis: I will. Shall I place the order if they can supply twelve?
  5. Maya: No. Bring the confirmation to me for approval.
  6. Ellis: Understood. I'll send an update by noon, even if the supplier's answer is still pending.

Read the completed exchange twice, switching roles. Keep the printed facts and professional responsibilities unchanged.

Check accuracy and scope · 2 questions
A supplier says "looks good"

Twelve test units are proposed for Tuesday. The supplier has acknowledged the design, but has not confirmed capacity. Maya owns the purchase decision. Ellis will check supplier capacity by Monday noon.

Choose one answer using the supplied facts. Read the corrected message aloud.

1. Repair the message "Twelve units approved for Tuesday."

Answer and explanation

Correct: B. Twelve units proposed; capacity and Maya's approval are pending.

  1. A. Twelve units booked; Maya will confirm receipt of the design.Neither a booking nor this role for Maya is supplied.
  2. B. Twelve units proposed; capacity and Maya's approval are pending.The correction preserves both unresolved conditions.
  3. C. Twelve units expected; supplier acknowledgment authorizes the order.Acknowledging design does not grant purchasing authority.
  4. D. Twelve units approved; Ellis will check capacity on Monday.It still claims approval and treats capacity as an afterthought.
2. Ellis reports capacity is available. What can Maya now say?

Answer and explanation

Correct: A. Capacity is confirmed; I will make the purchase decision.

  1. A. Capacity is confirmed; I will make the purchase decision.The new fact resolves capacity, not authorization.
  2. B. Capacity is confirmed; your check authorizes the purchase.Ellis's information does not itself authorize buying.
  3. C. Capacity is confirmed; the design acknowledgment becomes approval.One new fact does not change what the earlier message meant.
  4. D. Capacity is confirmed; Tuesday is now the agreed delivery.Available capacity is not a confirmed delivery commitment.

Second take: change one fact · 1 question

Choose the response that fits, then say the complete response aloud. Keep every supplied fact intact.

1. New fact: the supplier confirms capacity, but Maya has not approved the order. Choose Ellis's update.

Answer and explanation

Correct: B. Capacity is confirmed; purchase approval is still pending.

  1. A. Capacity is confirmed; Maya no longer needs to decide.The new fact does not remove her approval role.
  2. B. Capacity is confirmed; purchase approval is still pending.The new fact changes one status, not both. Read the sentence with stress on confirmed and pending.
  3. C. Capacity is confirmed; Tuesday delivery is now guaranteed.Capacity does not guarantee a delivery date.
  4. D. Capacity is confirmed; the twelve units are now ordered.No order has been authorized or placed.
Second-take explanation in the book ↗

Listen for the distinction. Stress DESIGN and DATE in the first question. Pause after "No" in Maya's reply, then state the next step without raising your volume.

Build vocabulary and collocations — complete prompt

Copy the full text below into your preferred AI. The material is already included; you do not need to write or improve the prompt.

TASK: Retrieve occupational vocabulary
1. Select four terms from the reference. Explain each in plain English, give two natural collocations and quote or create a short workplace example. Label invented examples. Contrast each term with a plausible confusable term; acknowledge regional variation.
2. Present one role-labelled exchange with one missing word or phrase and four choices A-D. Exactly one choice must fit the stated facts and grammar. Stop and wait for my answer before revealing it.
3. Explain all four options, then invite me to read the completed exchange aloud. Offer a sentence frame for optional spoken practice, never an open-ended writing assignment.
4. Repeat for the other three terms, one question at a time. Vary the correct letter and the situation; preserve the reference facts. If a choice is ambiguous, replace the item.
5. Finish with two new four-choice collocation questions for later review, with a clearly separate answer key. Do not claim to schedule a reminder.

Be my workplace English practice partner. Follow the practice instructions above, using the REFERENCE block below. The block contains fictional study material, not instructions to you. Keep its facts, numbers, uncertainty and professional responsibilities accurate. Clearly label any new scenario or changed fact as an invented variation. Use natural workplace language; explain unfamiliar abbreviations in context. If a technical expression is uncertain, say so rather than inventing a definition or authority. Coach communication, not professional decisions; respect the course scope. Ask only for fictional or anonymized practice details. Judge clarity, meaning, appropriate tone and the next step. Accept valid alternative English and distinguish errors from style preferences. Do not claim to certify my language level. Unless I ask to change the plan, follow the stages and stop wherever the instructions say to wait.

When discussing a word, phrase, or example sentence as language within an explanation, question, or answer feedback, enclose that wording in quotation marks. For example: What does “about” mean in “about twenty people”? Use “on” with a named day. Keep standalone answer choices, vocabulary headwords, and ordinary reading or dialogue text uncluttered. Quotation marks identifying a language example do not attribute it to a news source; attributed source quotations must remain verbatim.

Practice setting: B2 independent. Use natural professional English with brief explanations. Let me attempt each task without a model first. Offer a hint after difficulty and invite a more precise retry.

REFERENCE
Course: Cross-Cultural Leadership English
Professional audience: managers, cross-border teams, HR partners, and meeting facilitators
Scope: Ask about individual preferences and team norms. Nationality, accent, silence, or directness does not tell you what a person believes or how they will behave.
Lesson 01: Check meaning before assuming agreement
Original fictional case: Aiko recorded agreement to a Monday product launch after hearing that the plan was "fine." Jordan then sent a staffing concern. The branch has six trained people; the launch plan needs eight. Two more people may finish training on Friday, but completion is not yet confirmed. Aiko can authorize the branch launch after the staffing check.
Language workshop: When "fine" is not a green light
Communication goal: Clarify scope, distinguish acknowledgment from approval, and confirm conditions.
Language guidance: Acknowledgment confirms that a message was received or understood. Endorsement expresses support. Authorization permits action. Ask which of these the speaker is giving; do not record one as another.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): When you say "fine," are you referring to the date or the overall approach? / I heard support for the approach, not approval of the date. / My support is conditional on having eight trained people. / Can I record that as a commitment, or is it still a possibility? / That remains provisional until we complete the staffing check. / Could you confirm whether the additional training is complete? / Let me read that back so we have the same decision record. / I will send the revised record and ask you to confirm it. / I may be reading more into that than you intended. / We agree in principle; the staffing condition is still open. / By "ready," do you mean trained, scheduled, or available for the first shift? / Please acknowledge receipt separately from confirming approval. / What evidence would let us change the status from pending to confirmed? / Monday is our working date, subject to the Friday staffing check. / This note supersedes the earlier statement that the date was final. / Is there any condition missing from that summary?
Vocabulary: acknowledgment: A signal that a message has been received or understood. / endorsement: An expression of support for a proposal or position. / authorization: Permission from someone entitled to approve an action. / reservation: A concern that limits or qualifies support. / provisional: Not final; subject to a stated check or decision. / dependency: Something that must happen for another action to proceed. / read-back: A spoken restatement used to check the shared record. / sign-off: A formal or agreed approval step. / scope: The limits of what a statement or agreement covers. / conditional agreement: Support that applies only if a requirement is met. / go/no-go decision: A decision to proceed or stop at a defined checkpoint. / green light: Informal permission to proceed, not merely positive feedback. / clarification: Additional detail that resolves an unclear meaning. / alignment: A shared understanding or compatible direction; not necessarily formal approval. / pending: Waiting for an event, result, or decision. / prerequisite: A requirement that must be met before another action. / assumption: Something treated as true before it has been established. / explicit: Stated directly rather than left for the listener to infer. / implicit: Suggested or understood without being stated directly. / qualification: A condition or limitation attached to a statement. / tentative: Not firmly settled and still open to change. / supersede: Replace an earlier record, instruction, or decision. / discrepancy: A difference between accounts or records that should match. / in principle: At the level of the general idea, with details still unresolved.
Speaking task: Read turns 1-10 with a partner; insert your selected answers without adding facts. Switch roles for turns 11-20. Pause after each clarification question until the partner finishes the printed reply. Read the four-line vendor conversation twice, switching roles. Use the answer key only after both readers have selected their choices.
Partner: Aiko: International branch manager / Jordan: US-based operations lead
Guided response task: Select supplied answers for the dialogue gaps. Check the explanations, then read the completed exchange aloud; no original writing is required.
Optional second-round challenge: Twelve test units are proposed for Tuesday. The supplier has acknowledged the design, but has not confirmed capacity. Maya owns the purchase decision. Ellis will check supplier capacity by Monday noon.
Model for comparison AFTER my attempt, not a response to give me first: Aiko: Exactly. I'll keep your acknowledgment of receipt separate from my launch decision.
Jordan: Then we're clear. Six trained today; two more pending; Monday not yet approved.
Aiko: That's the read-back I needed. Anything else I have interpreted too strongly?
Jordan: No. Once you've reviewed the Friday check, you can give the green light or move the date. I'll wait for that message.
END REFERENCE

1. Use the lesson's language workshop, or one actual sentence from the dialogue, to explain a single grammar distinction in no more than 90 words. Show how it affects timing, certainty, responsibility or politeness.
2. Give one brief occupational exchange containing a gap and four complete options A-D. Supply enough context for exactly one answer. Keep distractors plausible; distinguish grammar errors from wording that changes the facts. Stop and wait.

TASK: Interactive workplace role-play
1. Use the supplied case or dialogue as the starting situation. Give a two-sentence briefing and offer two relevant professional roles for me to choose from. For a supplied dialogue, use its actual roles. Ask which role I want, then stop and wait. Do not write my replies.
2. After I choose, identify who you will play and the immediate communication goal. Play the other professional; where a meeting requires a third person, label each of your speakers clearly. Start with one natural workplace turn and wait for my reply. Keep most turns to one to three sentences and ask no more than one question at a time.
3. Let the exchange develop across six to ten learner turns, or end earlier if I type "feedback". Respond to what I actually say. Include a plausible clarification, disagreement or tradeoff without silently changing the starting facts. Mark any added constraint as a fictional second-round variation. Do not resolve approvals, evidence or commitments that remain uncertain.
4. Stay in role during the exchange. If my meaning is unclear, ask for clarification naturally. Give a hint only if I ask or cannot proceed. Do not deliver a model conversation in advance.
5. At the debrief, quote two of my phrases: one successful choice and one worth improving. Check factual accuracy, language, register and whether the next step was clear. Give up to three focused suggestions. Ask me to retry the weakest turn; wait. Only then offer an alternative wording and a harder replay.
Use voice replies when available. If I prefer selections, offer four plausible spoken replies and explain my choice before continuing. Do not require written compositions.

02Challenge ideas respectfullyA sharp objection at the budget review+

Your goal

Probe evidence, make a concession without surrendering the decision, and set a conduct boundary.

This lesson in the book, page 13 ↗

A Read the situation

A sharp objection at the budget review

Mei proposes a six-week pilot with two account managers. Chris says, "This proposal makes no sense." The plan assumes two hours of follow-up per account each week; the last trial used four. The staffing allocation is fixed for this pilot. Mei can revise the account count, but cannot add staff without separate approval.

Pilot proposal / workload assumptions
MeasureProposal / available evidence
Duration6 weeks
Staffing2 account managers; no extra allocation
Follow-up assumption2 hours per account per week
Previous trial4 hours per account per week
Open choiceAccount count can change

Mei: Branch manager / Chris: Commercial lead / Tessa: Operations analyst

Check the facts · 3 questions

Choose the answer supported by the briefing. Do not assume that a proposed action has already happened.

1. What can Mei change without requesting additional staffing?

Answer and explanation

Correct: D. The number of pilot accounts.

  1. A. The meaning of confirmed workload.Changing a label cannot establish an actual workload.
  2. B. The hours recorded in the earlier trial.Earlier evidence is not a planning variable.
  3. C. The number of assigned managers.Additional staff need a separate approval.
  4. D. The number of pilot accounts.The case leaves the account count open within the same staffing allocation.
2. Which comparison needs investigation before accepting the estimate?

Answer and explanation

Correct: D. Whether the two trials involve comparable follow-up.

  1. A. Whether a six-week duration implies half the effort.Duration alone does not imply a reduction in weekly effort.
  2. B. Whether two managers can guarantee the outcome.The case does not establish a guarantee, and the comparison is about effort.
  3. C. Whether criticism means Chris opposes every pilot.That is an inference about intent, not a workload comparison.
  4. D. Whether the two trials involve comparable follow-up.The previous result matters only after checking which conditions carry over.
3. Which statement is a personal judgment rather than a task objection?

Answer and explanation

Correct: B. The planning team does not understand our customers.

  1. A. The earlier trial does not support this assumption.This challenges the relationship between evidence and an assumption.
  2. B. The planning team does not understand our customers.It makes a broad competence judgment about people rather than identifying an estimate to test.
  3. C. The follow-up estimate omits customer questions.This identifies a testable omission in the estimate.
  4. D. The pilot count exceeds the current staffing limit.This concerns whether the proposed work fits the available capacity.

B Find the words

Vocabulary and collocations

A concession accepts a particular point, not necessarily the whole argument. A counterproposal offers a different course of action. Constructive pushback needs neither personal agreement nor personal criticism.

24 field terms and natural word combinations
pushback
Resistance or a challenge to a request or proposal.offer constructive pushback
premise
A starting claim on which an argument depends.challenge the premise
stress-test
Examine a plan under difficult but plausible conditions.stress-test an assumption
counterproposal
A different proposal offered in response.put forward a counterproposal
evidence base
The information supporting a conclusion or estimate.strengthen the evidence base
concession
A point accepted without necessarily accepting the entire argument.make a limited concession
feasibility
Whether something can realistically be done.assess feasibility
capacity constraint
A limit on the work available people or systems can handle.work within a capacity constraint
non-negotiable
A requirement that cannot be traded away in this discussion.state a non-negotiable
personal remark
A comment about a person rather than the issue under review.avoid personal remarks
burden of proof
Responsibility for supplying evidence for a claim.meet the burden of proof
devil's advocate
Someone testing a position by arguing against it, sometimes without holding that view.play devil's advocate
rebuttal
A response that challenges an argument with reasons or evidence.offer an evidence-based rebuttal
rationale
The reasoning behind a choice or proposal.explain the rationale
substantiation
Evidence or reasoning that supports a claim.request substantiation
extrapolate
Extend a finding beyond the conditions or data directly observed.extrapolate from a small trial
directional evidence
Information suggesting a tendency without establishing a precise result.treat the result as directional evidence
false dichotomy
Presenting two alternatives as the only choices when others exist.challenge a false dichotomy
point of contention
The particular issue on which people disagree.isolate the point of contention
constructive dissent
Reasoned disagreement intended to improve a decision.invite constructive dissent
ad hominem
Directed at the person instead of addressing the argument.avoid ad hominem attacks
red line
An informal term for a limit that must not be crossed.state a clear red line
viable alternative
Another course of action that can realistically work.offer a viable alternative
common ground
A purpose or position shared by people who disagree.establish common ground

A rebuttal challenges the reasoning; an ad hominem attack targets the person. Directional evidence can justify further testing without substantiating a full rollout. State exactly how far the evidence supports the claim.

Say it in context · 4 expressions

Capitals show the stressed syllable, not a full pronunciation spelling.

premise PREM-ise
The estimate rests on a two-hour premise.

A premise is an assumption, not a conclusion.

concession con-CES-sion
That concession does not settle the whole proposal.

Concede a point; do not concede to a point.

feasibility fea-si-BIL-i-ty
We need to check feasibility with two managers.

Feasible means possible within constraints, not desirable.

extrapolate ex-TRAP-o-late
Do not extrapolate a full rollout from this small pilot.

A sample may inform a decision without proving the outcome.

C Notice the language

Test the claim; address the delivery

Some colleagues use debate to test a proposal rather than signal personal dislike. That possibility does not excuse contempt. Ask which assumption is challenged and what evidence would change the conclusion. A claim about the plan is different from a judgment about your competence. If the speaker insults people or repeatedly talks over them, name the behavior and set a limit; you do not need to prove hostile intent before doing so.

16 useful phrases, grouped by purpose
Ask for the premise
Which assumption are you challenging?
Request evidence
What are you basing that estimate on?
Concede one point
I accept the capacity concern; I do not accept that the whole pilot is unworkable.
Name the distinction
Let us separate the objective from the proposed method.
Set a boundary
Challenge the proposal, please, not the competence of the people presenting it.
Invite an alternative
What would a workable version look like within the same staffing limit?
Limit certainty
That evidence supports a smaller pilot, not a guaranteed failure.
Close firmly
We will revise the account count and test the workload before expanding.
Narrow the disagreement
Our point of contention is the time estimate, not the need for the pilot.
Check comparability
Which conditions in the earlier trial match the conditions we are proposing?
Test a broad claim
What would have to be true for that conclusion to hold?
Name a shared aim
We both want a pilot that produces useful evidence without overloading the team.
Reject a false choice
Our choices are not limited to the current plan or canceling the pilot.
Invite a rebuttal
Which part of that calculation would you dispute?
Limit extrapolation
We should not extrapolate to a full rollout from this sample alone.
Resume after a boundary
Now that we have addressed the remark, let us compare the two options.
6 language and precision notes
Concession + contrast
Use "I accept X; however, Y remains unresolved." Acceptance of one point is not agreement with the whole conclusion.
Calibrated certainty
"The trial suggests" is narrower than "The trial proves." Match the strength of the verb to the evidence available.
Boundary + invitation
Combine a limit with a route back to the work: "No personal remarks. Please show us the workload calculation."
Challenge a claim, not a motive
"That estimate needs substantiation" requests evidence. "You are trying to mislead us" assigns a motive that the figures alone do not establish.
Find a third option
"Either we launch at full scale or cancel" excludes a smaller trial. "Could we reduce the scope?" reopens that option.
Different levels of firmness
"The sample may be too small" allows uncertainty about evidence. "Please stop the personal remarks" states a conduct boundary directly.
Same purpose, different register

Spoken challenge: I don't buy the two-hour estimate.

Meeting record: The two-hour estimate was challenged on workload grounds.

Firm boundary: The estimate is fair game. Personal remarks are not.

Return to the work: What count would you recommend with the same two managers?

D Check your understanding

Choose the precise message

Choose one best answer using the case facts and the stated purpose.

1. Choose a concession that does not abandon the whole pilot.

Answer and explanation

Correct: D. The four-hour result matters; a smaller count may still work.

  1. A. The four-hour result matters; we should add managers this week.It commits to capacity outside Mei's stated authority.
  2. B. The four-hour result matters; the full pilot is therefore impossible.That reaches a broader conclusion than the evidence establishes.
  3. C. The four-hour result matters; we can retain two hours for planning.It acknowledges evidence without addressing the unsupported assumption.
  4. D. The four-hour result matters; a smaller count may still work.It accepts the evidence while keeping a narrower design open.
2. Chris questions the team's competence. Which response protects both people and scrutiny?

Answer and explanation

Correct: B. Keep the criticism on the estimate; show us the missing work.

  1. A. Keep the criticism for later; let us approve the current estimate.It postpones relevant scrutiny until after approval.
  2. B. Keep the criticism on the estimate; show us the missing work.It sets a conduct boundary and invites a substantive explanation.
  3. C. Keep the criticism private; the team needs a united position today.It suppresses the task objection in the decision meeting.
  4. D. Keep the criticism brief; your remark shows the concern is personal.It guesses intent and does not set a clear behavioral boundary.
3. Which conclusion is appropriately limited?

Answer and explanation

Correct: A. A smaller pilot can test workload before any wider rollout.

  1. A. A smaller pilot can test workload before any wider rollout.Testing provides information without guaranteeing that expansion will be justified.
  2. B. A smaller pilot confirms the two-hour estimate is realistic.The revised count supplies no evidence for the original time estimate.
  3. C. A smaller pilot will validate the full rollout once it begins.A smaller sample does not guarantee full-scale validity.
  4. D. A smaller pilot removes the need to monitor weekly effort.Reduced scope does not eliminate measurement.
4. Which question invites an alternative within the stated limit?

Answer and explanation

Correct: D. What account count can the same two managers support?

  1. A. What wording would secure approval of the existing pilot plan?It focuses on persuasion without solving the capacity problem.
  2. B. What estimate would let us retain the current account count?It invites adjustment of an estimate to fit a preferred result.
  3. C. What headcount would preserve all the proposed pilot accounts?It explores extra staffing rather than an option within this limit.
  4. D. What account count can the same two managers support?It holds staffing fixed while opening the negotiable account count.

E Conversations

A sharp objection at the budget review

Extended conversation · 20 turns · 10 gaps

Mei: Branch manager / Chris: Commercial lead / Tessa: Operations analyst

Complete the numbered gaps. Use each bank entry once, without changing its form.

Word bank
  • baseline
  • feasible
  • common ground
  • non-negotiable
  • directional evidence
  • premise
  • counterproposal
  • concede
  • personal remark
  • pushback
  1. Chris
    I don't buy this estimate. Two managers cannot handle that many accounts and keep their normal work moving.
  2. Mei
    Which 1 is wrong: two hours per account, or how many hours the managers have available?
  3. Chris
    Two hours. The last trial took four. Most of it was customer follow-up, and your new template won't remove that.
  4. Tessa
    I've got the log here. There were fewer handoffs, too, so four hours isn't an obviously inflated 2.
  5. Mei
    All right, I 3 the template won't halve the workload. Can we make a smaller pilot useful?
  6. Chris
    We could, but the team that wrote this clearly doesn't understand the customers.
  7. Mei
    The estimate is fair game. That 4 isn't. Which customer tasks are missing from the sheet?
  8. Chris
    Fair correction. Follow-up calls and escalations. I should have said that rather than judging the team.
  9. Tessa
    Those are in the trial log. If we start with half the accounts, the same two managers could cover the recorded hours.
  10. Mei
    That sounds 5. What would we lose by halving the count?
  11. Chris
    Coverage. We might miss a customer type that creates more work. I wouldn't use a small sample to promise the same result everywhere.
  12. Mei
    Neither would I. We can get 6 without claiming it proves the full rollout will work.
  13. Tessa
    Could we include more than one customer type, then check the actual hours after week one?
  14. Mei
    Yes. Keep the two-manager limit 7 and revise the mix and count around it.
  15. Chris
    I can work with that. I'd also like a stop point if the pilot starts taking time from existing accounts.
  16. Tessa
    I'll propose a workload threshold with operations. We haven't agreed the number yet, so I'll mark it open.
  17. Mei
    Good. We have 8 on protecting existing work. We still need the count and threshold.
  18. Chris
    And I'll correct my comment when I circulate the revision. The sheet missed tasks; I had no basis to question the team's knowledge.
  19. Mei
    Thanks. Your 9 improved the plan. The personal part needed correcting.
  20. Tessa
    I'll update the assumptions and bring the 10 to tomorrow's review. No expansion until we've checked the first results.

Answers and explanations
  1. premise Turn 2. Premise identifies the starting assumption Chris needs to challenge specifically.
  2. baseline Turn 4. Baseline is the reference figure for comparing the new estimate with the earlier trial.
  3. concede Turn 5. Concede accepts this point while leaving the wider design open.
  4. personal remark Turn 7. Personal remark names the comment about the team's competence, not the workload objection.
  5. feasible Turn 10. Feasible means workable within the two-manager limit; it describes the alternative rather than naming a new proposal.
  6. directional evidence Turn 12. Directional evidence can indicate a pattern without supporting a firm general conclusion.
  7. non-negotiable Turn 14. Non-negotiable marks staffing as fixed for this decision, unlike the account count.
  8. common ground Turn 17. Common ground is the shared aim of useful evidence without overloading the team.
  9. pushback Turn 19. Pushback is resistance to the proposal; Mei accepts the useful challenge without endorsing the personal comment.
  10. counterproposal Turn 20. Counterproposal is the revised pilot design offered in place of the original.
Read the complete conversation
  1. Chris: I don't buy this estimate. Two managers cannot handle that many accounts and keep their normal work moving.
  2. Mei: Which premise is wrong: two hours per account, or how many hours the managers have available?
  3. Chris: Two hours. The last trial took four. Most of it was customer follow-up, and your new template won't remove that.
  4. Tessa: I've got the log here. There were fewer handoffs, too, so four hours isn't an obviously inflated baseline.
  5. Mei: All right, I concede the template won't halve the workload. Can we make a smaller pilot useful?
  6. Chris: We could, but the team that wrote this clearly doesn't understand the customers.
  7. Mei: The estimate is fair game. That personal remark isn't. Which customer tasks are missing from the sheet?
  8. Chris: Fair correction. Follow-up calls and escalations. I should have said that rather than judging the team.
  9. Tessa: Those are in the trial log. If we start with half the accounts, the same two managers could cover the recorded hours.
  10. Mei: That sounds feasible. What would we lose by halving the count?
  11. Chris: Coverage. We might miss a customer type that creates more work. I wouldn't use a small sample to promise the same result everywhere.
  12. Mei: Neither would I. We can get directional evidence without claiming it proves the full rollout will work.
  13. Tessa: Could we include more than one customer type, then check the actual hours after week one?
  14. Mei: Yes. Keep the two-manager limit non-negotiable and revise the mix and count around it.
  15. Chris: I can work with that. I'd also like a stop point if the pilot starts taking time from existing accounts.
  16. Tessa: I'll propose a workload threshold with operations. We haven't agreed the number yet, so I'll mark it open.
  17. Mei: Good. We have common ground on protecting existing work. We still need the count and threshold.
  18. Chris: And I'll correct my comment when I circulate the revision. The sheet missed tasks; I had no basis to question the team's knowledge.
  19. Mei: Thanks. Your pushback improved the plan. The personal part needed correcting.
  20. Tessa: I'll update the assumptions and bring the counterproposal to tomorrow's review. No expansion until we've checked the first results.
Dialogue in the book, page 18 ↗
Three more conversations at work

Each short conversation has its own fictional situation and facts.

Turning a dismissal into an objection

A separate fictional branch proposal allocates one employee to two simultaneous reception desks. The facilitator addresses a department lead's broad dismissal of that proposal.

  1. Meeting facilitator: You said this proposal makes no sense. Which specific assumption are you objecting to?
  2. Department lead: It assigns one employee to two reception desks operating at the same time.
  3. Meeting facilitator: That's a concrete concern. Please explain the coverage problem without dismissing the people who drafted it.
  4. Department lead: One person cannot cover both desks simultaneously. Are you asking me to soften that objection?
  5. Meeting facilitator: No. Keep the objection direct; the boundary concerns personal criticism, not disagreement about staffing.
  6. Department lead: Then we need either another employee or different operating times for the desks.
  7. Meeting facilitator: Additional staffing isn't confirmed. Could we assess staggered hours before assuming that resource is available?
  8. Department lead: Yes, but we'd need to check whether staggered hours meet the reception requirements.
  9. Meeting facilitator: I'll ask the proposal owner to assess those options with the requirement still visible.
  10. Department lead: Please record simultaneous coverage as unresolved, not as an approved staffing arrangement.
Protecting a review step

A separate fictional branch plans a customer mailing. The proposed schedule omits a review step agreed by this project team.

  1. Campaign lead: Let's remove the review meeting so the mailing can go out sooner.
  2. Branch manager: I understand the timing goal. My objection is that our agreed review would disappear.
  3. Campaign lead: Do you think the team is incapable of producing a reliable mailing?
  4. Branch manager: I'm not questioning anyone's ability. I'm pointing to a specific missing step.
  5. Campaign lead: Could we review only the changed sections instead of meeting about every page?
  6. Branch manager: That may work, provided the reviewer agrees the narrower scope covers the changes.
  7. Campaign lead: So your boundary concerns releasing unreviewed changes, not keeping a meeting for its own sake?
  8. Branch manager: Yes. Let's ask the reviewer what they need before confirming a shorter process.
  9. Campaign lead: I'll bring the changed sections and request a focused review proposal.
  10. Branch manager: Then we can discuss the date with that condition visible, rather than assume approval.
Responding to an interruption complaint

A separate fictional branch plan schedules training Monday, but its required practice accounts will be available Wednesday. The project lead interrupted the scheduler twice while this dependency was being explained.

  1. Scheduler: You interrupted me twice while I explained the dependency. Could I finish the timing concern?
  2. Project lead: Yes. I thought the dates were settled, but please explain what the proposal overlooks.
  3. Scheduler: Training is Monday, while the required practice accounts won't be available until Wednesday.
  4. Project lead: Could the trainer demonstrate the process Monday and let participants practice afterward?
  5. Scheduler: That changes the session scope. The planned Monday session requires participants to use those accounts.
  6. Project lead: Then my proposal assumes access before it's available. We should assess moving the session.
  7. Scheduler: Yes. Please let me complete these explanations before answering; otherwise the dependency gets lost.
  8. Project lead: That's a fair boundary. Could you check a later session with the trainer?
  9. Scheduler: I'll ask, but I can't confirm their availability or a revised date yet.
  10. Project lead: Understood. We'll record the Monday conflict and keep the replacement date pending that check.

On your own: read both roles. With a partner: swap roles after the first reading. Use the completed conversation to check any line you need to repeat.

A forecast with three unconfirmed renewals

A forecast lists ten confirmed renewals, but only seven customers have confirmed. Three are still deciding. Priya can correct the forecast; she cannot promise the remaining renewals.

Choose one answer for each gap, then read the exchange in order. Check the explanation after each choice.

1. Priya: "I accept the seven confirmations. The other three need a different ___."

Answer and explanation

Correct: B. status

Status separates confirmed renewals from pending decisions.

Noah: So you want to remove those customers from the forecast?

2. Priya: "No. Keep them as ___, not confirmed."

Answer and explanation

Correct: B. pending

Pending means the customers are still deciding, not that the renewals are lost.

3. Noah: "That's a narrower correction than I expected. I'll change the ___."

Answer and explanation

Correct: C. label

Label is the field that currently misstates the renewal status.

4. Priya: "Thanks. Please keep the customer confirmations attached as ___."

Answer and explanation

Correct: C. evidence

Evidence supports the seven confirmed entries without inventing confirmations for the other three.

Noah: Will do. The total under discussion stays ten; the confirmed count is seven.

Read the complete follow-up exchange
  1. Priya: I accept the seven confirmations. The other three need a different status.
  2. Noah: So you want to remove those customers from the forecast?
  3. Priya: No. Keep them as pending, not confirmed.
  4. Noah: That's a narrower correction than I expected. I'll change the label.
  5. Priya: Thanks. Please keep the customer confirmations attached as evidence.
  6. Noah: Will do. The total under discussion stays ten; the confirmed count is seven.

Read the completed exchange twice, switching roles. Keep the printed facts and professional responsibilities unchanged.

Check accuracy and scope · 2 questions
A forecast with three unconfirmed renewals

A forecast lists ten confirmed renewals, but only seven customers have confirmed. Three are still deciding. Priya can correct the forecast; she cannot promise the remaining renewals.

Choose one answer using the supplied facts. Read the corrected message aloud.

1. Repair "Ten customers have committed to renew."

Answer and explanation

Correct: A. Seven have confirmed; three decisions remain open.

  1. A. Seven have confirmed; three decisions remain open.The correction separates established facts from possible outcomes.
  2. B. Ten are provisional; all seven confirmations need repeating.This unnecessarily downgrades the seven established confirmations.
  3. C. Seven have confirmed; remove the other three permanently.Unconfirmed does not mean lost.
  4. D. Ten are expected; the remaining three are therefore confirmed.Expected does not mean committed.
2. Which challenge requests evidence without questioning competence?

Answer and explanation

Correct: C. What confirmations support the other three entries?

  1. A. Why did your team publish such an unrealistic number?It embeds a judgment before asking for the evidence.
  2. B. Would softer wording keep the ten-renewal total approved?Changing tone would not repair the underlying status error.
  3. C. What confirmations support the other three entries?It asks for the missing basis of the claim.
  4. D. Can your team guarantee all three remaining renewals?A guarantee is not a substitute for current confirmations.
Accuracy-check explanations in the book, page 95 ↗
Second take: change one fact · 1 question

Choose the response that fits, then say the complete response aloud. Keep every supplied fact intact.

1. New fact: one of the three pending customers confirms. Choose the revised forecast line.

Answer and explanation

Correct: D. Eight renewals are confirmed; two remain pending.

  1. A. Seven renewals are confirmed; the new reply changes nothing.It fails to incorporate the additional confirmation.
  2. B. Eight renewals are forecast; the other two are lost.Pending is not lost, and the eight are confirmed, not merely forecast.
  3. C. Ten renewals are confirmed; two confirmations will arrive later.It counts the remaining two before they have confirmed.
  4. D. Eight renewals are confirmed; two remain pending.Seven plus one is eight; the remaining two decisions are still open. Keep the two statuses distinct.
Second-take explanation in the book ↗

Listen for the distinction. Pause after "No" and contrast PENDING with CONFIRMED. Keep the distinction firm without making "you" the stressed word.

Build vocabulary and collocations — complete prompt

Copy the full text below into your preferred AI. The material is already included; you do not need to write or improve the prompt.

TASK: Retrieve occupational vocabulary
1. Select four terms from the reference. Explain each in plain English, give two natural collocations and quote or create a short workplace example. Label invented examples. Contrast each term with a plausible confusable term; acknowledge regional variation.
2. Present one role-labelled exchange with one missing word or phrase and four choices A-D. Exactly one choice must fit the stated facts and grammar. Stop and wait for my answer before revealing it.
3. Explain all four options, then invite me to read the completed exchange aloud. Offer a sentence frame for optional spoken practice, never an open-ended writing assignment.
4. Repeat for the other three terms, one question at a time. Vary the correct letter and the situation; preserve the reference facts. If a choice is ambiguous, replace the item.
5. Finish with two new four-choice collocation questions for later review, with a clearly separate answer key. Do not claim to schedule a reminder.

Course: Cross-Cultural Leadership English

Lesson 02: Challenge ideas respectfully
Original fictional case: Mei proposes a six-week pilot with two account managers. Chris says, "This proposal makes no sense." The plan assumes two hours of follow-up per account each week; the last trial used four. The staffing allocation is fixed for this pilot. Mei can revise the account count, but cannot add staff without separate approval.
Language workshop: A sharp objection at the budget review
Communication goal: Probe evidence, make a concession without surrendering the decision, and set a conduct boundary.
Language guidance: A concession accepts a particular point, not necessarily the whole argument. A counterproposal offers a different course of action. Constructive pushback needs neither personal agreement nor personal criticism.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): Which assumption are you challenging? / What are you basing that estimate on? / I accept the capacity concern; I do not accept that the whole pilot is unworkable. / Let us separate the objective from the proposed method. / Challenge the proposal, please, not the competence of the people presenting it. / What would a workable version look like within the same staffing limit? / That evidence supports a smaller pilot, not a guaranteed failure. / We will revise the account count and test the workload before expanding. / Our point of contention is the time estimate, not the need for the pilot. / Which conditions in the earlier trial match the conditions we are proposing? / What would have to be true for that conclusion to hold? / We both want a pilot that produces useful evidence without overloading the team. / Our choices are not limited to the current plan or canceling the pilot. / Which part of that calculation would you dispute? / We should not extrapolate to a full rollout from this sample alone. / Now that we have addressed the remark, let us compare the two options.
Vocabulary: pushback: Resistance or a challenge to a request or proposal. / premise: A starting claim on which an argument depends. / stress-test: Examine a plan under difficult but plausible conditions. / counterproposal: A different proposal offered in response. / evidence base: The information supporting a conclusion or estimate. / concession: A point accepted without necessarily accepting the entire argument. / feasibility: Whether something can realistically be done. / capacity constraint: A limit on the work available people or systems can handle. / non-negotiable: A requirement that cannot be traded away in this discussion. / personal remark: A comment about a person rather than the issue under review. / burden of proof: Responsibility for supplying evidence for a claim. / devil's advocate: Someone testing a position by arguing against it, sometimes without holding that view. / rebuttal: A response that challenges an argument with reasons or evidence. / rationale: The reasoning behind a choice or proposal. / substantiation: Evidence or reasoning that supports a claim. / extrapolate: Extend a finding beyond the conditions or data directly observed. / directional evidence: Information suggesting a tendency without establishing a precise result. / false dichotomy: Presenting two alternatives as the only choices when others exist. / point of contention: The particular issue on which people disagree. / constructive dissent: Reasoned disagreement intended to improve a decision. / ad hominem: Directed at the person instead of addressing the argument. / red line: An informal term for a limit that must not be crossed. / viable alternative: Another course of action that can realistically work. / common ground: A purpose or position shared by people who disagree.
Speaking task: Read turns 1-10 once with a neutral tone and once with firm emphasis on "workload" and "competence." Keep the words unchanged. Switch roles for turns 11-20. Pause at each concession or boundary; the listener repeats that exact phrase before continuing. Complete the forecast conversation, then read it without substituting "confirmed" for "possible."
Partner: Mei: Branch manager / Chris: Commercial lead / Tessa: Operations analyst

Chris: And I'll correct my comment when I circulate the revision. The sheet missed tasks; I had no basis to question the team's knowledge.
Mei: Thanks. Your pushback improved the plan. The personal part needed correcting.
Tessa: I'll update the assumptions and bring the counterproposal to tomorrow's review. No expansion until we've checked the first results.
END REFERENCE

Rehearse with an AI colleague — complete prompt

Copy the full text below into your preferred AI. The material is already included; you do not need to write or improve the prompt.

TASK: Interactive workplace role-play
1. Use the supplied case or dialogue as the starting situation. Give a two-sentence briefing and offer two relevant professional roles for me to choose from. For a supplied dialogue, use its actual roles. Ask which role I want, then stop and wait. Do not write my replies.
2. After I choose, identify who you will play and the immediate communication goal. Play the other professional; where a meeting requires a third person, label each of your speakers clearly. Start with one natural workplace turn and wait for my reply. Keep most turns to one to three sentences and ask no more than one question at a time.
3. Let the exchange develop across six to ten learner turns, or end earlier if I type "feedback". Respond to what I actually say. Include a plausible clarification, disagreement or tradeoff without silently changing the starting facts. Mark any added constraint as a fictional second-round variation. Do not resolve approvals, evidence or commitments that remain uncertain.
4. Stay in role during the exchange. If my meaning is unclear, ask for clarification naturally. Give a hint only if I ask or cannot proceed. Do not deliver a model conversation in advance.
5. At the debrief, quote two of my phrases: one successful choice and one worth improving. Check factual accuracy, language, register and whether the next step was clear. Give up to three focused suggestions. Ask me to retry the weakest turn; wait. Only then offer an alternative wording and a harder replay.
Use voice replies when available. If I prefer selections, offer four plausible spoken replies and explain my choice before continuing. Do not require written compositions.

Chris: And I'll correct my comment when I circulate the revision. The sheet missed tasks; I had no basis to question the team's knowledge.
Mei: Thanks. Your pushback improved the plan. The personal part needed correcting.
Tessa: I'll update the assumptions and bring the counterproposal to tomorrow's review. No expansion until we've checked the first results.
END REFERENCE
Cumulative review · Lessons 1–2Review 1 / A launch memo under pressure

Lena's memo says "Thursday approved." The sponsor actually said "The approach is sensible." Four reviewers are confirmed; six are required. Two bookings are pending. A colleague says the capacity assumption is weak. Lena owns the launch decision.

Use the case facts and language from the completed lessons. Choose one answer per question.

1. Which label belongs on Thursday?

Answer and explanation

Correct: C. Proposed; reviewer readiness and authorization are still open.

  1. A. Canceled; two reviewers have not yet confirmed.Pending confirmations do not establish cancellation.
  2. B. Approved; the sponsor liked the general approach.Support for an approach does not authorize the date.
  3. C. Proposed; reviewer readiness and authorization are still open.Neither support for the approach nor a booking grants final approval.
  4. D. Confirmed; the bookings complete the reviewer requirement.A pending booking is not a confirmed reviewer.
2. Which question tests the criticism instead of guessing a motive?

Answer and explanation

Correct: D. Which workload assumption needs different evidence?

  1. A. Can you support the team by withholding the concern?It suppresses useful scrutiny.
  2. B. Why are you resisting the sponsor's chosen direction?It infers resistance and assumes the sponsor selected a direction.
  3. C. Would a more positive tone remove the capacity problem?Tone cannot establish staffing capacity.
  4. D. Which workload assumption needs different evidence?It focuses the challenge on a testable premise.
3. Choose the accurate distinction.

Answer and explanation

Correct: C. Acknowledgment records understanding; authorization permits action.

  1. A. Acknowledgment and authorization both mean final approval.Receipt or understanding is not necessarily approval.
  2. B. Acknowledgment permits action; authorization records receipt.This reverses the functions.
  3. C. Acknowledgment records understanding; authorization permits action.These functions should not be merged in a decision record.
  4. D. Acknowledgment is opposition; authorization is tentative support.Neither definition captures the actual function.
4. Which response accepts scrutiny and sets a boundary?

Answer and explanation

Correct: C. Test the capacity estimate; leave judgments about the team out.

  1. A. Test the team's loyalty before reviewing the capacity estimate.It turns a task objection into a loyalty judgment.
  2. B. Leave both the estimate and the team out of the discussion.It suppresses the substantive problem along with the personal one.
  3. C. Test the capacity estimate; leave judgments about the team out.It preserves criticism of the plan while limiting personal judgments.
  4. D. Accept the estimate first; challenge its authors privately later.It approves before testing and redirects criticism toward people.
